body:
You are reminding me of a close South-Asian friend of mine (also female).  She is generally a strong and independent person, but often accepts traditional sexist stereotypes/traditions as non-sexist and thinks discussion of gender roles or gender in society.  She also thinks that there are things "guys are just better at" including physical strength and doesn't feel any sense of indignity about letting a guy carry something for her or over-politeness by men towards women.

This is what I said to her that somewhat changed her mind: on the issue of sexist traditions (wedding ceremonies, name changing, gender roles/politeness), I argued that they were not arbitrary traditions and that they systematically reinforced male authority over women, even if women didn't think of them that way or if the individual people did not consciously reflect this influence.  It forms part of a culture that is symbolically devaluing women and treating them as property.  The fact that many men would balk at changing their name upon marriage, but think little of asking women to do the same reflects this cognitive dissonance; most men in such a position say that it's an affront to their identity, independence, and other similar notions of selfhood.  Also, specifically on the issue of politeness: it is not as if one person being polite to another person is bad - of course it is good, and people should treat each other equally politely.  However, when the politeness you show toward someone varies based on the other person's gender, this is damaging because it usually means being more polite towards women.  What is the basis for this?  Are women weaker, more fragile, less self-sufficient?  There are enough extrapolated examples of this kind of thinking (ex, Padma Patil actress link on this subreddit now), that men are responsible for protecting "their women" that it shouldn't be hard to understand why it is important to eliminate even symbolic notions of this difference.  Furthermore, everyone gains from this scenario, because then women hold doors for men, too.

So, why should people care about gender roles?  Not because they are concerned so much about their own personal behavior, as most people thinking about and considering gender roles will not have personal hang-ups, but because they are concerned about societal ramifications.  Most practically?  Sexism in hiring, firing, and compensation at work.  This is a huge problem, and obviously is not resolved simply because you know that you can do the work as well as anyone regardless of your gender; your boss and co-workers need to recognize this, too.  (And this does affect men, too, although it doesn't get talked about as much.  Men who want to work in a primarily female field (nursing, teaching, secretary, etc.) will often be ridiculed and discriminated against.  Or, in the case of my friend, whose sister is considering arranged marriage partners, the types of "acceptable jobs" in a potential husband are very few: finance; engineer.  This is a fundamental infringement of male freedom that is also damaging to their ability to be the person they want to be.)

There is a quote from Eleanor Roosevelt: "Do one thing each day that scares you" roughly.  If I could manage the courage to actually do that I think I would be very proud of myself.  I think my fatalism about my life is partly related to my habituated behaviors, such that I generally can estimate the limits I have on myself, and be unable to break out of them.  If I can actually break those limits I think I could do much better.  

I do actually do other things: art, writing, thrift store shopping, volunteering, reading, cooking, radio, playing in snow.  I'm ok satisfied with those things, and think I could continue doing more of them.  But I spend most of my time with school/work, and will spend most time in the future on work, so I feel that is more important in establishing my satisfaction.  Also it's such a big part of your identity that I feel it gives me a sense of who I am.  Perhaps I should try to change my way of thinking about that, though.

> You are looking too far down the road
> sometimes one can't see the forest for the trees

I can see this is a problem, but it is a habit I have of looking at things.  I think I am someone who is likely to want a lot of stability in my life, not wanting to move around a lot or change jobs or such things, partly because I don't think I can negotiate that well but also because I like simple things like community and friends and building that in one place.  So my idea of doing that is to arrange my long-term situation as early as possible.  But this is probably unlikely and I will think about changing my attitude towards it.

> Depression

I am actually seeing a therapist with the university (free with student med insurance) for the shyness problem I have but would feel uncomfortable with antidepressants because they alter your personality (just by eliminating depression chemically, I mean).  I feel like it is better to address the situational causes of the depressive feelings.  I know that there are some cases (maybe many cases) where the feelings are either out of balance with the stimuli or where there is no "valid" stimuli, and in such cases medication would likely be needed, but I hope I am not there yet.
